name: Anything
description:
Write any valid lambda-calculus expression. It can be a variable, a function, or an application.

Examples: x, \x.x, or (\x.x) y.

This first exercise checks that your expression is well-formed; it does not require a particular result.

name: Identity
description:
Write a function that returns its input unchanged.

This is the simplest possible lambda function. Just pass through the argument.

name: True Function
description:
Write a function that takes TWO arguments and returns the FIRST one.

Remember: In lambda calculus, a function that takes multiple arguments is written with nested lambdas.
For example: \x.\y.BODY takes two arguments (first x, then y), and BODY can use both.

So write a function where the body just returns the first argument, ignoring the second.

name: False Function
description:
Write a function that takes TWO arguments and returns the SECOND one.

Similar to the TRUE function, but this time ignore the first argument and return the second.

Remember: \x.\y.BODY is a two-argument function (takes x, then y).

name: Create a Pair
description:
Write a function that creates a pair from two elements.

A pair is a function that takes a selector function and applies it to both elements.
In other words: PAIR A B should reduce to \f.f A B

This means:
- PAIR takes two arguments: A and B
- It returns a function that takes one more argument (f)
- That function applies f to both A and B

IMPORTANT: Note how application is left-associative and greedy!
- f A B means (f A) B, NOT f (A B)
- If you write \f.f A B, the body 'f A B' will apply f to A first, then apply that result to B
- That's exactly what we want for a pair!

Test examples:
- PAIR x y reduces to \f.f x y
- Then if you apply it to TRUE (which returns first arg), you get x
- If you apply it to FALSE (which returns second arg), you get y

name: First Element of Pair
description:
Extract the first element from a pair.

You've already written functions that select the first argument (TRUE) and can create pairs (PAIR).
FST should take a pair and apply the "select first" function to it.

name: Second Element of Pair
description:
Extract the second element from a pair.

Similar to FST, but extract the second element. You have FALSE which selects the second argument.

name: Simple List
description:
A simple list can be built from pairs. The empty list is FALSE, and a non-empty list is a PAIR containing its first element and the rest of the list.

For example, a list of two elements is PAIR first (PAIR second FALSE).

Write a function that takes a list of five elements and returns its third element. You can use PAIR to build lists and FST and SCD to inspect them.

tests.input: (PAIR a (PAIR b (PAIR c (PAIR d (PAIR e FALSE)))))
(PAIR red (PAIR green (PAIR blue (PAIR white (PAIR black FALSE)))))

name: Any True in a List
description:
Write a function that takes a list of three Church booleans and returns TRUE if at least one item is TRUE. It should return FALSE when all three items are FALSE.

The list is encoded with PAIR and ends with FALSE. Inspect each element with FST and move through the list with SCD. Combine the results with OR.

name: Push onto a List
description:
Write a function that takes an element and a list, then returns a new list with that element at the front.

For example, PUSH apple (PAIR banana FALSE) should produce PAIR apple (PAIR banana FALSE). The list is encoded as nested PAIRs and FALSE represents the empty list.

name: Pop from a List
description:
Write a function that takes a non-empty list and returns its tail: the list containing every element except the first.

For example, POP (PAIR apple (PAIR banana FALSE)) should produce PAIR banana FALSE. When the input has just one item, its tail is the empty list FALSE.

name: Is the List Empty?
description:
Write a function that takes a list and returns TRUE if it is empty, or FALSE if it contains at least one item.

The empty list is FALSE. A non-empty list is a pair, which can be used as a selector: apply the list to a handler for its head and tail, then to the empty-case result.

name: Creating Recursion
description:
Write the Y combinator: a function that takes a function F and returns a fixed point of F.

For any suitable F, Y F reduces to F (Y F). That lets F call itself recursively. The Y combinator itself is a valid expression even though applying it to some functions can continue forever; these tests use recursive functions that reach a base case.

tests.input: (\recur.\lst.lst (\head.\tail.\dummy.recur tail) TRUE) (PAIR A (PAIR B (PAIR C FALSE)))

name: Strip a Boolean Prefix
description:
Write a recursive function that removes all FALSE values from the beginning of a list of booleans and returns the remaining list. The list is guaranteed to contain at least one TRUE.

For example, [FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE] becomes [TRUE, FALSE], while [TRUE, FALSE] is unchanged. Use Y to define the recursion.

tests.input: (PAIR FALSE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE (PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE FALSE))))) TRUE
(PAIR FALSE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE (PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE FALSE))))) FALSE TRUE
(PAIR FALSE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE (PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE FALSE))))) FALSE FALSE TRUE

name: Accumulate a List
description:
Write a function ACC that takes a list L, a two-argument combining function F, and an initial value I.

Starting with I, apply F to the accumulated value and each list element in turn. Return the final accumulated value. For example, accumulating OR from FALSE over [TRUE, FALSE] returns TRUE; accumulating over an empty list returns the initial value.

tests.input: (PAIR FALSE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR FALSE FALSE))) OR FALSE
(PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE FALSE))) XOR FALSE

name: All True in a List
description: Write a function that takes a list of booleans and returns TRUE only if every item is TRUE. The empty list should return TRUE: every item in an empty list satisfies the condition.

name: Map a Function over a List
description:
Write MAP to take a list L and a function F, and return a list containing F applied to each element of L.

For example, mapping NOT over [TRUE, FALSE] returns [FALSE, TRUE]. The empty list maps to the empty list.

tests.input: (PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE FALSE))) NOT TRUE
(PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE FALSE))) NOT FALSE TRUE

name: No True Values
description: Write a function that takes a list of booleans and returns TRUE if every item is FALSE, and FALSE if any item is TRUE. The empty list returns TRUE.

name: Filter a List
description:
Write FILTER to take a list L and a predicate F, and return the list of elements for which F returns TRUE. The predicate always returns a Church boolean.

For example, filtering [TRUE, FALSE, TRUE] with the identity function returns [TRUE, TRUE].

tests.input: (PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE FALSE))) (\value.value) FALSE TRUE

name: Zip Two Lists
description:
Write ZIP to take two lists of equal length and return a list of pairs, combining corresponding elements.

For example, ZIP [A, B] [C, D] returns [(A, C), (B, D)].

tests.input: (PAIR A (PAIR B FALSE)) (PAIR C (PAIR D FALSE)) TRUE TRUE
(PAIR A (PAIR B FALSE)) (PAIR C (PAIR D FALSE)) TRUE FALSE
(PAIR A (PAIR B FALSE)) (PAIR C (PAIR D FALSE)) FALSE TRUE TRUE
(PAIR A (PAIR B FALSE)) (PAIR C (PAIR D FALSE)) FALSE TRUE FALSE

name: Compare Boolean Lists
description: Write EQBLIST to compare two boolean lists of equal length. Return TRUE if they contain the same values in the same order, and FALSE otherwise.

tests.input: (PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE FALSE)) (PAIR (OR TRUE FALSE) (PAIR (AND TRUE FALSE) FALSE))
(PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE FALSE)) (PAIR TRUE (PAIR TRUE FALSE))
(PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE (PAIR TRUE FALSE)))) (PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE (PAIR TRUE (PAIR FALSE FALSE))))

name: Concatenate Lists
description:
Write CONCAT to join two lists, keeping all elements of the first list before all elements of the second.

For example, CONCAT [A, B] [C] returns [A, B, C].

tests.input: (PAIR A (PAIR B FALSE)) (PAIR C FALSE) TRUE
(PAIR A (PAIR B FALSE)) (PAIR C FALSE) FALSE TRUE
(PAIR A (PAIR B FALSE)) (PAIR C FALSE) FALSE FALSE TRUE

name: Reverse a List
description: Write REVERSE to return a list with its elements in reverse order. The empty list and single-element lists should also work.

tests.input: (PAIR A (PAIR B (PAIR C FALSE))) FALSE TRUE
(PAIR A (PAIR B (PAIR C FALSE))) FALSE FALSE TRUE

name: Swap Arguments
description:
Write a function that takes two arguments and returns them in reverse order.

SWAP A B should evaluate to B A

This requires careful use of bracketing since application is left-associative.

name: Apply Twice
description:
Write a function that takes a function F and a value V, and applies F to V twice.

SQR F V should evaluate to F (F V)

Note the brackets! F F V (without brackets) would mean (F F) V due to left-associativity.
You need F (F V) to apply F to the result of F V.

name: Swap a Function's Arguments
description:
Write a function that takes a two-argument function F and two values A and B, then applies F to B and A in that order.

INDIRECTION F A B should evaluate to F B A.

This differs from SWAP: SWAP returns its two inputs in reverse order, while this challenge swaps the arguments passed to another function.

name: Conditional
description:
Write a function that takes THREE arguments: a boolean, a value if true, and a value if false.

IF BOOLEAN A B should:
- Reduce to A if BOOLEAN is TRUE
- Reduce to B if BOOLEAN is FALSE

Remember: TRUE and FALSE are functions that select their first or second argument respectively.

name: Boolean NOT
description:
Write a function that negates a boolean.

NOT TRUE should reduce to FALSE
NOT FALSE should reduce to TRUE

Think about what TRUE and FALSE do - they select arguments. Can you use IF to implement NOT?

name: Boolean AND
description:
Write a function that performs logical AND on two booleans.

AND should take two boolean arguments and:
- Return TRUE only if both are TRUE
- Return FALSE otherwise

Think about what each boolean does and how you can chain them.

name: Boolean OR
description:
Write a function that performs logical OR on two booleans.

OR should take two boolean arguments and:
- Return FALSE only if both are FALSE
- Return TRUE otherwise

Similar to AND, but think about the logic differently.

name: Boolean XOR
description:
Write a function that performs logical XOR (exclusive or) on two booleans.

XOR should take two boolean arguments and:
- Return TRUE if exactly one of them is TRUE
- Return FALSE otherwise

This one is trickier! Think about combining AND, OR, and NOT.
